title: Metabolic States
objectives: Compare hormonal regulation in fed vs. fasted states
Trace the timeline of metabolic adaptations during starvation
Analyze clinical disorders of metabolic state transitions

fed_state.title: The Fed (Postprandial) State
fed_state.content:
0-4 Hours After Eating

1. Hormonal Profile

  • ↑Insulin (pancreatic β-cells)
  • ↓Glucagon
  • Amylin (slows gastric emptying)

2. Key Metabolic Pathways

  • Liver: Glycogenesis, lipogenesis
  • Muscle: Glucose uptake (GLUT4), glycogenesis
  • Adipose: LPL activation → TAG storage

Clinical Correlation: Insulinoma

  • Persistent insulin secretion → hypoglycemia
  • Whipple's triad: Low glucose, neuro symptoms, relief with glucose

postabsorptive.title: Postabsorptive State (4-12 Hours)
postabsorptive.content:
Transition to Fasting

1. Hormonal Shifts

  • ↓Insulin, ↑Glucagon
  • Mild ↑Cortisol

2. Metabolic Adaptations

  • Liver: Glycogenolysis → gluconeogenesis
  • Adipose: HSL activation → FFA release
  • Muscle: Switches to fatty acid oxidation

3. Brain Fuel

  • Exclusively glucose (not yet ketone-adapted)

early_starvation.title: Early Starvation (12-48 Hours)
early_starvation.content:
Phase 1: Glycogen Depletion

1. Hormonal Changes

  • ↑↑Glucagon, ↑Cortisol
  • ↓Insulin to basal levels

2. Tissue Responses

  • Liver: Maximal gluconeogenesis (alanine/lactate)
  • Muscle: Protein catabolism → amino acid release
  • Adipose: Lipolysis → ↑FFAs

Clinical Correlation: Diabetic Ketoacidosis

  • Uncontrolled lipolysis → ketone overproduction
  • Metabolic acidosis (pH <7.3, ↓HCO3-)
  • Treatment: Insulin + fluids

prolonged_starvation.title: Prolonged Starvation (>48 Hours)
prolonged_starvation.content:
Phase 2: Protein Sparing

1. Metabolic Priorities

  • Liver: Ketogenesis (from FFAs)
  • Brain: Adapts to use ketones (50-75% of energy)
  • Muscle: ↓Protein breakdown (conserves lean mass)

2. Hormonal Adaptations

  • ↑Growth hormone (protein sparing)
  • ↓T3 (reduces basal metabolic rate)

3. Renal Role

  • Gluconeogenesis from glutamine
  • Ketone excretion (conserves Na+/K+)

Clinical Correlation: Anorexia Nervosa

  • Adapted ketosis → paradoxical energy
  • Cardiac risks (hypokalemia, QT prolongation)

refeeding.title: Refeeding Syndrome
refeeding.content:
Transition Back to Fed State

1. Metabolic Risks

  • Hypophosphatemia: ↑Insulin drives phosphate into cells
  • Hypokalemia: K+ shifts intracellularly
  • Fluid retention (↑ADH)

2. Clinical Management

  • Slow carbohydrate reintroduction
  • Aggressive electrolyte repletion (PO43-, K+, Mg2+)
  • Thiamine prophylaxis (Wernicke's risk)

At-Risk Populations

  • Chronic malnutrition (alcoholism, anorexia)
  • Post-bariatric surgery
  • Prolonged NPO status

faqs.title: FAQs
faqs.content:
FAQs

Q: Why does the brain take 3-5 days to use ketones? +

A: Ketone transporter (MCT1) upregulation requires time. Initially, neurons rely on glucose to avoid disrupting neurotransmission (GABA/glutamate balance).

Q: How does cortisol differ from glucagon in fasting? +

A: Glucagon acts acutely (minutes) on liver glycogenolysis, while cortisol promotes sustained gluconeogenesis (hours-days) via enzyme induction and muscle protein breakdown.

Q: Why is refeeding syndrome lethal? +

A> Rapid insulin surge depletes serum PO43- → impaired ATP synthesis → cardiac/respiratory failure. Hypokalemia → fatal arrhythmias.
